doc.title: Cal Collins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 11, 1997

title: The 1950s, rock and roll and discovering bebop
summary: Rock and roll pushed big band and jazz aside, while he loved bebop and heard Parker and Miles.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Right, fortunately. We look back on the 50s as an age of innocence I suppose, and somewhat prosperity after the war. Do the 50s seem like that to you?

Yeah, they did — yeah, they did. I never had any problem, before I went into the Army and after I was in the Army, I didn’t have too much problem getting work. But the Bill Haley and the Comets, and all that rock & roll really got into it as far as popularity was concerned I think. Real good music, big band and jazz and all of that sort of faded from the limelight, and here comes Elvis and all that.
Right, and at the same time you had jazz turning to bebop I guess somewhat. © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

Oh, I was really into that. I loved that change, it just fit, it seemed like it just fit me just perfectly. Yeah, I really liked that. I can remember the first times that I heard people like Parker and Miles and some of those people. And then later on of course some of the real good tenor players, I loved them, Stan Getz and all that thing. But I don’t know, the bebop was a new direction for the music, and I loved it, still do. I consider myself a bebop player I guess.
